passage:
Warden's note, Zainab.

For the last week I have seen Aditi's light on at 3 a.m. at the end of the corridor. Today at breakfast Aditi's eyes were red and hands unsteady on the tea cup. When I asked, Aditi said, "There's a man online who says awful things about women's hostels. I keep replying. He never changes his mind but I can't stop." The thread was long, each reply sharper than the last. Aditi said the anger felt like it was eating at Aditi's head.

I did not tell Aditi to stop caring. I asked, "Does this help anyone, including you?" Aditi thought and said no. We agreed on phones off at 11 p.m. and one offline step: drafting a letter to the hostel committee about the dark path to the gate.

I will check the corridor light tonight.

qa.q: What time was Aditi's light on?
qa.a: Aditi's light was on at 3 a.m.

qa.q: How was Aditi feeling about the argument, and what shows it?
qa.a: Angry and hurt, and unable to stop: red eyes, unsteady hands, and words that the anger felt like it was eating at Aditi's head.

qa.q: What did Zainab suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Zainab asked whether the arguing helped anyone including Aditi, agreed a phone-off time, and offered an offline step, a letter about the dark path, which puts the energy where it can change something.

qa.q: How might the man online see the thread?
qa.a: He likely sees one more argument to win and will not change his mind, which is why more replies serve nobody.

grounding: Aditi stays up arguing with a stranger who will not change his mind, and the warden helps Aditi disengage and turn the energy to offline action.

passage:
Monday, 2:15 am. Jeevan's laptop glowed in the dark hostel room. The stranger on the metro-fare thread had called him "a spoilt kid" again, and Jeevan was on his fourth long reply, full of statistics and sarcasm. His jaw ached from clenching.

Wednesday. He slept through his nine o'clock class. At lunch Alka waved a hand in front of his face. "You're arguing with someone called MetroMan77? Has he ever changed his mind once?" Jeevan opened his mouth, then shut it. The answer was no. And his own replies had got meaner.

Saturday. He muted the thread. Instead, he and Alka went to the ward office with a printed letter asking for a student fare pass, signed by forty hostel residents. It took an hour. The clerk stamped it and said it would go to the committee.

qa.q: How many hostel residents signed the letter?
qa.a: Forty hostel residents signed the letter.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling during the Monday night argument, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Jeevan felt angry and hostile; his clenched jaw and fourth sarcastic reply at 2:15 am show how caught up he was.

qa.q: Which choice worked better, and why?
qa.a: Muting the thread and taking a signed letter to the ward office worked better, because it used his energy where it could actually change something.

qa.q: How does Alka see Jeevan's late-night arguing?
qa.a: Alka sees it as a draining fight with someone who never changes, and she can see it costing Jeevan sleep and making him meaner.

grounding: The three beats show a student caught in endless online arguments who disengages and puts his energy into offline action.

passage:
Sit, Zeenat, let your uncle tell you something. When I was twenty, in 2003, the internet was new for us. There was a cricket forum, and one man there, calling himself TigerFan, said our college team cheated. I stayed up night after night in the cyber café near the bus stand, spending my pocket money by the hour, typing long angry answers. My roommate Hasan would come to drag me back and I'd shout at him.

One night Hasan asked me, "Imran bhai, who is reading this? Him? He'll never agree." I felt foolish, and tired, deep tired.

Next morning I stopped. I used those evenings to coach the juniors' team instead. Two of those boys played for the district later. TigerFan? I don't even remember his real argument. So your phone at two in the morning, beta, think about Hasan's question.

qa.q: Where did Imran stay up typing angry answers?
qa.a: Imran stayed up in the cyber café near the bus stand.

qa.q: What did Imran feel when Hasan asked who was reading the arguments?
qa.a: Imran felt foolish and deeply tired, realising the arguing had drained him without convincing anyone.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the difference?
qa.a: Imran's choice to stop the next morning and coach the juniors' team turned the wasted nights into something that mattered.

qa.q: How might Hasan have felt during those nights?
qa.a: Hasan probably felt worried and frustrated, since his roommate was shouting at him and losing sleep over a stranger.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young man stuck arguing online with a stranger who disengages and spends his energy on offline action.
